questions.q: Is there already a registration or ticketing system (or a tool you pay for) that holds the attendee list, and does it offer check-in? Have you looked at off-the-shelf check-in apps, and what budget do you have?
questions.why: High uncertainty × high impact: buying or switching on an existing feature could remove the need to build, and the budget sizes everything else.

questions.q: Where does the attendee list come from today, and how is it kept up to date? Can it still change on the day (walk-ins, substitutions, cancellations, name corrections)?
questions.why: The upstream origin of the list decides whether this is a simple import or a live-sync and on-the-spot-registration subsystem.

questions.q: Will the venue entrance have reliable internet? Should the app keep working if the connection drops (offline, with check-ins synced later)?
questions.why: Offline versus online-only are two different architectures; it is the most common unstated assumption.

questions.q: How many entrances and staff devices will be scanning at once, how many attendees are expected, and how fast must a check-in be at the peak (e.g. in the 20 minutes before the opening)?
questions.why: Concurrency across doors and peak throughput are functional requirements that shape the design.

questions.q: What does a second scan of the same person mean: refuse it as a duplicate, allow re-entry after stepping out, or record entry to another zone or session? Do attendee categories (VIP, press, speaker) get different treatment?
questions.why: Check-in is not a boolean; each meaning is a different data model.

questions.q: How is a person identified at the door: scanning a QR code/badge, searching by name, or both? What happens when someone has no code or is not on the list?
questions.why: Scanning fails in real conditions; the manual fallback is a meaningful share of arrivals and must be scoped.

questions.q: Is this for a single event, or should it be reusable for future events? When is the event date?
questions.why: Throwaway versus reusable kit changes the data model and cost, and the fixed date sets the scope line.

questions.q: How is check-in handled today (paper list, spreadsheet, another app), and what went wrong that triggered this request?
questions.why: The real problem and as-is process tell us what must actually improve.

questions.q: What do you need afterwards from the data (live headcount, attendance export, who gets it, e.g. sponsors) and which devices will staff use (own phones, tablets)?
questions.why: Attendance data is usually the post-event deliverable, and the devices bound what is possible; GDPR limits what can be shared.

briefs.problem: Door staff need a fast, reliable way to identify arriving attendees and record who actually came, on a date that cannot move.
briefs.solution: A simple check-in app for door staff that identifies attendees by scan or name search, records arrival, and gives the client a headcount and an attendance record afterwards.
introduces: an attendee list that must stay current up to and during the event
multi-device check-in with a defined outcome for the same person processed twice
an identification fallback path (name search, on-the-spot registration)
possibly an offline mode with local attendee snapshot and later sync
an attendance record and export that becomes the post-event deliverable

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A custom app is needed to check attendees in at the entrance.
challenges.alternative: If the attendee list already lives in a registration or ticketing tool, switching on its check-in feature, or buying an off-the-shelf check-in app, may cover the need for a fraction of the effort and with less day-of risk.
challenges.consequence: Building a custom app against a fixed date means paying for scanning, sync, fallback and rehearsal work that a proven tool may already provide.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what tool holds the attendee list, whether it offers check-in, and which off-the-shelf options were considered and why they were rejected.

challenges.headline: Check-in as a simple scan
challenges.premise: Checking in means scanning a code and marking a person as arrived.
challenges.alternative: Treat identification as a degrading path (scan, then name search, then on-the-spot registration) and treat check-in as an event that can mean duplicate, re-entry or another zone, rather than a single yes/no flag.
challenges.consequence: A scan-only, one-flag design fails at the door when codes won't read, names are misspelled or someone arrives as a substitute, and it produces unreliable attendance data afterwards.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client what a second scan means and scope the manual fallback as core, not an extra.

challenges.headline: Assuming connectivity at the door
challenges.premise: The app can rely on the venue network being available during peak arrival.
challenges.alternative: Decide explicitly between online-only and offline-capable. Offline means a local snapshot of the list and later sync, which is a different architecture, not a setting.
challenges.consequence: Discovering poor signal on the day produces a queue in front of the client with no time to rebuild.
challenges.recommendation: Ask about venue connectivity now and, if uncertain, plan an on-site test before choosing the architecture.

page.title: Check first whether you need to build a check-in app
page.recommendation: Before committing to a custom build, decide whether an existing registration tool or an off-the-shelf check-in app can cover door check-in. We recommend answering that first, and only building if it cannot, with a deliberately simple app focused on a reliable door.
page.why: Your request describes a solution, not the underlying need, and nothing tells us what holds your attendee list today or what was already considered. The event day is fixed and a failure shows up as a queue in front of your own guests, so the safest and cheapest path may be a proven tool. If a build is justified, a narrow scope with a manual fallback beats a feature-rich one.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost driver is making check-in dependable across several doors and devices, and above all whether it must keep working offline. The risk that matters most is a failure at the door on the day, with no chance to fix it afterwards.

open.question: Is there already a registration or ticketing system that holds the attendee list, does it offer check-in, and what budget do you have?
open.would_change: If it already offers check-in, or a suitable off-the-shelf app fits the budget, we would recommend not building at all.

open.question: Will the venue entrance have reliable internet, and when is the event?
open.would_change: Unreliable connectivity means an offline-capable build with later sync, which is materially more costly; the date sets how much scope fits.

open.question: What should a second scan of the same person do (refuse, allow re-entry, record another zone), and do VIP, press or speaker categories get different treatment?
open.would_change: Anything beyond a simple duplicate block changes the data model and the amount of build.

open.question: Where does the attendee list come from, and can it still change on the day through walk-ins, substitutions or corrections?
open.would_change: A list that keeps changing requires on-the-spot registration and live updates rather than a single import.

open.question: How many entrances, staff and expected attendees will there be, and what check-in speed do you need at peak?
open.would_change: Several simultaneous doors and a tight peak target raise the cost of concurrency handling and device testing.

open.question: Is this for one event or should it be reusable for future events?
open.would_change: A reusable kit needs a multi-event data model and configuration, increasing cost compared with a one-off app.

briefs.problem: Entrance staff need to identify arriving attendees quickly and record their arrival on a fixed event day, without queues at the door and with a reliable attendance record afterwards.
briefs.solution: A staff-facing check-in app for the event entrance: attendee list, fast scan with a manual name-search fallback, arrival recording, a live count and a post-event attendance export.
introduces: An attendee list that stays live up to and during the event (walk-ins, substitutions, cancellations)
A check-in recording model that defines duplicate, re-entry and other-zone scans
A multi-device consistency layer for several entrances scanning at once
A manual fallback path for every scan failure, including on-the-spot registration
A post-event attendance export that serves as a client deliverable

challenges.headline: Build rather than reuse a tool
challenges.premise: A custom app is the right answer to checking attendees in at the door.
challenges.alternative: If the attendee list already lives in a registration or ticketing platform, that platform's check-in feature or an off-the-shelf event check-in app may cover the need. Configuring it and rehearsing would then replace the build.
challenges.consequence: Building a check-in app with offline support, sync and conflict handling is real effort. Doing it when an existing licence or a purchasable tool already covers it spends budget and schedule on something the client may already own.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, confirm what registration or ticketing tool is in use and what it can do at the door. Build only for the gaps it leaves.

challenges.headline: Assumed single, simple check-in
challenges.premise: Checking in means one scan per person at one door.
challenges.alternative: Treat a second scan as one of three distinct outcomes, decided up front: a duplicate to block, a re-entry to allow, or access to another zone or session to record separately. Start with the narrowest meaning the client confirms, such as one entry per event, and keep the model able to grow.
challenges.consequence: A model built for a single boolean has to be reworked if the client later wants re-entry or room-level access. Two devices scanning the same person within seconds also produce undefined behavior unless the outcome is chosen in advance.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to state what a second scan should do, and choose the entry model before building.

complexity_reasons: Offline capability, if required, means a local snapshot plus later sync with conflict rules
Several entrances scanning the same attendee concurrently
A list that keeps changing up to the day
Hard date with a venue rehearsal inside the scope
briefs.cost_driver: Whether check-in must work offline and sync across devices
risks: Weak or no connectivity at the entrance can stop check-in if the app assumes it is always online.
A queue at the peak arrival window, since throughput per attendee has not been specified or measured on real devices.
Untrained or temporary staff using the app for the first time that morning, often one-handed.
The attendee list changing late, so a frozen import is edited by hand at the door.
Attendee personal data and what sponsors may receive afterwards fall under GDPR.

opportunities.text: Design the Event, Attendee, Category and Check-in model so a second event reuses it with different lists, branding and categories, even if the first build is a one-off.
Make the manual name search and on-site registration a first-class path, so it covers failed scans, misspelled names and walk-ins with one mechanism.

next_steps: Identify any registration or ticketing platform and check-in tool already in use or paid for, and decide build versus configure.
Fix the event date, the expected attendee volume, the number of entrances and the venue connectivity, so the offline decision can be made.
Have the client define what a second scan means and what staff do for someone not on the list.
If building, deliver the core check-in loop with manual fallback first, then rehearse on the real devices at the venue before the date.

decisions.decision: Treat this as a commissioned internal tool, with no revenue model or user acquisition work.
decisions.why: The request is phrased as an organisational need for staff.

decisions.decision: Every scan path has a manual fallback through name search and on-the-spot registration.
decisions.why: Scanning will fail on the day in real conditions, and the queue at the door happens in front of the client.
decisions.alternative: Scan-only flow with escalation to a supervisor.
decisions.tradeoff: Some extra build effort, in exchange for a door that keeps moving when scans fail.

page.title: Build a check-in app, or use what you have?
page.recommendation: Before committing to a build, decide whether an existing registration or ticketing tool can already check attendees in at the door. We recommend confirming that first. If it cannot, build a small check-in app with a manual name-search fallback, a live count and a post-event export, and rehearse it at the venue before the event date.
page.why: The event date cannot move and the cost of a failure is a queue in front of your client. A tool you already own or can buy removes both the build effort and the risk of a new system. If a build is needed, the highest-value parts are the ones that keep the door moving when something goes wrong: a name search for failed scans and a way to register someone on the spot.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is making check-in work reliably across several entrances, and offline if the venue has weak signal. The risk that matters most is a queue at the peak arrival window if the flow is slow or the network drops. Both are settled by rehearsing on the real devices at the venue.

open.question: Do you already use a registration or ticketing platform with a check-in feature, and what budget applies to this?
open.would_change: If a tool already covers it, we would configure it and drop most of the build.

open.question: What is the event date, how reliable is the signal at the entrance, and which devices will staff use?
open.would_change: Poor signal means check-in must work offline, which adds a local copy of the list and later syncing.

open.question: Where does the attendee list come from, and will it keep changing on the day?
open.would_change: A list that keeps changing requires a live update path and on-site registration rather than a one-time import.

open.question: Is this for one event only, or should it be reusable for future events?
open.would_change: A reusable kit needs configurable lists, branding and categories, which raises the cost.

open.question: What should a second scan do: block, allow re-entry, or record entry to another room or session? And what should staff do for someone not on the list?
open.would_change: Re-entry or room-level access changes the data model, not just a rule.

open.question: Who works the door, and are they trained staff or temporary hostesses seeing the app that morning?
open.would_change: Untrained operators call for a simpler interface and more of the effort on usability.

open.question: What are the expected attendee numbers, the number of entrances, and the target time per person at peak?
open.would_change: High volumes with several doors raise the need for concurrent scanning and speed tuning.

open.question: Who needs the attendance data afterwards, and in what format?
open.would_change: A sponsor-facing export adds format requirements and limits on what personal data can be shared.

open.question: What should happen when a person is not on the list, a name is misspelled, a registration was cancelled, or a device or the network fails mid-check-in?
open.would_change: If walk-ins, substitutions or cancelled registrations must be handled at the door, on-site registration and a defined refusal or escalation path become mandatory scope rather than an extra.

assumptions.text: The app is a commissioned internal tool, so no revenue model or user acquisition is involved.
Door operators may be untrained, so the interface must work without training.
Attendance data will be needed after the event as a deliverable.
The attendee list is not final and will change up to and during the event day.
Staff can check in and search attendees, while managers see live counts and exports.

briefs.problem: Staff need to identify arriving attendees and record their arrival at the entrance quickly and reliably on a fixed event day, and the client ends up with a trustworthy attendance record. The underlying need itself is deduced, not stated.
briefs.solution: A simple, training-free check-in app for door staff: an imported attendee list, scan or name-search identification, a recorded arrival per person, a manual fallback, a live count and a post-event export.
introduces: an attendee list that can be imported and still edited on the day
a check-in record with defined duplicate and re-entry outcomes
a local copy of the list on each device with later synchronisation (if offline use is required)
a name search and on-the-spot registration path for arrivals who do not scan
a live arrival count and a post-event attendance export carrying personal data

challenges.headline: Building before checking existing tools
challenges.premise: A custom app is needed for check-in on the event day.
challenges.alternative: If the event already has a registration or ticketing tool with a scanning feature, switching it on, or renting an off-the-shelf check-in app for one event, delivers the same door function without a build or a rehearsal of new code.
challenges.consequence: Building something that a licensed or purchasable tool already does spends the budget and the limited time before an immovable date on a path where a failure means a queue in front of the client.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what registration or ticketing tool is in use, whether it has check-in, and what was tried and rejected. Build only for the gap that remains.

challenges.headline: Assuming connectivity at the door
challenges.premise: The request describes scanning at the entrance and says nothing about the network, so a connected app is implicitly assumed.
challenges.alternative: Deciding offline behaviour first: either require a proven connection at each entrance, or keep a local copy of the list on each device that synchronises later.
challenges.consequence: Online-only fails exactly when the room fills and the network saturates. Offline capability added late is a different architecture, and cannot be fixed on the day.
challenges.recommendation: Ask about the venue network and devices now. If connectivity is not proven, treat offline operation, with a printed list as the last fallback, as part of the core scope.

challenges.headline: What 'checked in' means
challenges.premise: Check-in is a single yes/no arrival record per attendee.
challenges.alternative: Define the second scan explicitly: refuse it, allow it as re-entry, or record it as access to a different zone or session. If only a single arrival is needed, the simplest rule (warn on a second scan, never block) keeps the data model small.
challenges.consequence: Each meaning implies a different data model, and the wrong choice shows up as wrong attendance numbers or as staff turning people away at the door.
challenges.recommendation: Agree one rule for the first release in writing with the event manager, and keep zones and sessions out unless the event truly needs them.

complexity_reasons: offline operation and synchronisation, if required
several devices at several entrances handling the same person
a list that keeps changing up to and during the event
a fixed date with a required rehearsal
briefs.cost_driver: offline capability and multi-device consistency at the door
risks: A queue at the door at peak arrival if the check-in flow takes more than a few seconds per person on the real devices.
Loss of connectivity at the venue with no offline mode or fallback in place.
The same attendee processed on two devices within seconds, giving wrong counts or an argument at the door.
Untrained staff seeing the app for the first time on the morning of the event.
Personal data in the list and in the export (and what sponsors may receive) raises GDPR obligations that are not yet scoped.

opportunities.text: Keep the attendee, category and check-in model generic and event-agnostic so the same core can serve a later event as a reusable kit, while only building event-specific branding and fields now.
Treat the attendance export as a first-class deliverable from the start, with a defined format and agreed recipients, rather than a post-event extraction.

next_steps: Establish what registration or ticketing tool and check-in feature already exist, and the budget, before designing anything.
Confirm the event date, the number of attendees, entrances and staff, the venue network and the devices.
Agree the check-in rule (duplicate, re-entry, zone) and the fallback for arrivals who do not scan, and write them down as acceptance scenarios.
If a build is still justified, plan a minimal check-in core plus a rehearsal at the venue on the real devices, with a printed list as backup.

decisions.decision: Treat this as a single known event with a fixed date, not a product to sell.
decisions.why: The request refers to "the event day" and describes staff as the users.
decisions.tradeoff: Lower cost and faster delivery now, in exchange for rework if a second event follows.

decisions.decision: Include a manual fallback (name search, on-the-spot registration, printed list) in scope from the start.
decisions.why: Scanning fails in real conditions and the date cannot move.
decisions.alternative: Scan-only flow with manual handling left to staff.
decisions.tradeoff: More to build and rehearse, in exchange for no stalled door.

page.title: Build a check-in app, or use what exists?
page.recommendation: Before committing to a build, confirm whether your registration or ticketing tool, or a rented off-the-shelf check-in app, already does this. If a gap remains, we recommend a minimal check-in app for this one event: an imported attendee list, scan and name search, a defined rule for repeat scans, a manual fallback, and a rehearsal at the venue.
page.why: Your request fixes a solution but not the need, and the event date cannot move. A tool that already exists would remove both the cost and the risk of new code failing in front of your guests. If a build is needed, the door is the one place where failure is visible immediately, so the fallback and the rehearsal matter more than extra features.
page.cost_and_risk: The main driver of effort is working reliably when the network is poor and several staff scan at once. The risk that matters most is a queue at the door at peak arrival, especially with untrained staff on devices not tested in the venue.

open.question: Do you already use a registration or ticketing tool with a check-in feature, and what budget applies?
open.would_change: If one exists, we recommend using it and building nothing, or only a small gap-filler.

open.question: Must check-in keep working if the venue network drops, and which devices will staff use?
open.would_change: If yes, offline operation becomes core scope and raises the build size and the rehearsal needs.

open.question: Is this one event or the start of a reusable tool, and what is the event date?
open.would_change: A reusable tool justifies a more general design; a near date forces a smaller scope.

open.question: What does "checked in" mean when the same person is scanned twice, or enters different zones?
open.would_change: Zones or re-entry tracking make the data model and the staff guidance larger.

open.question: Where does the attendee list come from, how large is it, and can it change on the day?
open.would_change: A list that keeps moving needs editing and on-site registration, not just an import.

open.question: How do staff identify people, and what happens for someone with no code, a misspelled name, or not on the list?
open.would_change: A large share of non-scanning arrivals makes the fallback path a main part of the build.

open.question: How many entrances, staff and arrivals in the busiest 20 minutes, and how many seconds per person is acceptable?
open.would_change: A tight seconds-per-person target changes the interface and the number of devices.

open.question: How is check-in done today and what went wrong?
open.would_change: It may show the real problem is elsewhere, or that the existing method is an adequate fallback.

assumptions.text: This is a single known event with a fixed date, commissioned or internal, not a product to sell.
The operators are untrained staff at one or more entrances.
The attendee list is imported from elsewhere and will keep changing until the event day.
An attendance report or export after the event is expected as a deliverable.
Attendee data is personal data under GDPR and the export must respect its limits.
